method: read-only researcher fetched primary sources; an independent read-only skeptic re-fetched every URL and tried to refute each claim
searched: WebSearch: Kelley Meka 2023 arXiv strong bounds Roth theorem three-term arithmetic progressions
WebSearch: Leng Sah Sawhney 2024 Improved bounds for Szemeredi's theorem arXiv
WebSearch: erdosproblems.com forum problem 3 arithmetic progressions divergent reciprocal sum
WebSearch: r_4(N) OR r4(N) improved bound 2024 2025 Green-Tao polylogarithmic
WebSearch: Erdos conjecture arithmetic progressions reciprocal sum resolved 2025 2026 proof
WebSearch: Erdos problem 3 OR Erdos-Turan conjecture arXiv 2026 progress r_k(N)

claims.claim: Erdos Problem 3 is OPEN, with a $5000 prize attached, as stated on erdosproblems.com.
claims.quote: If $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}=\infty$ then must $A$ contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions? [Status: OPEN, $5000 prize]
claims.skeptic_note: Fetched erdosproblems.com/3. Page states exactly: "OPEN This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation. - $5000" alongside the problem statement quoted in the claim. Status and prize amount match exactly.

claims.topic: Erdos Problem 3 - stronger form and k=3 partial resolution
claims.claim: Erdos's stronger quantitative conjecture is that r_k(N) <<_C N/(log N)^C for every C>0, and the page states this is now known for k=3.
claims.formula: r_k(N) ≪_C N/(log N)^C for every C>0
claims.quote: Erdős...conjectures that $r_k(N) \ll_C\frac{N}{(\log N)^C}$ for every $C>0$ (now known for $k=3$)
claims.skeptic_note: Fetched erdosproblems.com/3. Page states: Erdős conjectured 'r_k(N) \ll_C N/(\log N)^C for every C>0' (now proven for k=3), matching the claim's formula and the 'now known for k=3' assertion verbatim in substance.

claims.claim: Bloom and Sisask (2020) proved the first non-trivial case (k=3) of Erdos's conjecture, showing 3-AP-free sets have size O(N/(log N)^(1+c)).
claims.formula: |A| ≪ N/(log N)^{1+c} for some absolute constant c>0
claims.citation: Thomas F. Bloom, Olof Sisask, "Breaking the logarithmic barrier in Roth's theorem on arithmetic progressions," arXiv:2007.03528 (2020)
claims.quote: We show that if $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ contains no non-trivial three-term arithmetic progressions then $\lvert A\rvert \ll N/(\log N)^{1+c}$ for some absolute constant $c>0$. In particular, this proves the first non-trivial case of a conjecture of Erdős on arithmetic progressions.
claims.skeptic_note: Fetched arxiv.org/abs/2007.03528. Abstract reads verbatim: 'if A is a subset of {1,...,N} contains no non-trivial three-term arithmetic progressions then |A| << N/(log N)^{1+c} for some absolute constant c>0... this proves the first non-trivial case of a conjecture of Erdos on arithmetic progressions.' Exact match to quote and formula.

claims.topic: Kelley-Meka 2023 - best known bound for r_3(N)
claims.claim: Kelley and Meka (2023) proved any 3-AP-free subset of {1,...,N} has size at most N times a bound of the form 2^{-O((log N)^β)}, a super-polynomial-in-log improvement over the earlier N/(log N)^{1+c} bound.
claims.formula: |A| ≤ 2^{-O((\log N)^\beta)} \cdot N for some \beta>0 (i.e. r_3(N) ≪ 2^{-\Omega((\log N)^\beta)} N)
claims.citation: Zander Kelley, Raghu Meka, "Strong Bounds for 3-Progressions," arXiv:2302.05537 (2023); presented at FOCS 2023
claims.quote: We show that for some constant $\beta > 0$, any subset $A$ of integers $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ of size at least $2^{-O((\log N)^\beta)} \cdot N$ contains a non-trivial three-term arithmetic progression. Previously, three-term arithmetic progressions were known to exist only for sets of size at least $N/(\log N)^{1 + c}$ for a constant $c > 0$.
claims.skeptic_note: Fetched arxiv.org/abs/2302.05537. Abstract confirms verbatim: 'any subset A of integers {1,...,N} of size at least 2^{-O((log N)^beta)} * N contains a non-trivial three-term arithmetic progression. Previously ... N/(log N)^{1+c}.' Formula and comparison to prior bound match exactly.

claims.claim: Bloom and Sisask (2023) modified the Kelley-Meka method to obtain an explicit exponent: 3-AP-free sets have size at most exp(-c(log N)^{1/9})N.
claims.citation: Thomas F. Bloom, Olof Sisask, "An improvement to the Kelley-Meka bounds on three-term arithmetic progressions," arXiv:2309.02353 (2023)
claims.quote: proving that if $A\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$ has no non-trivial three-term arithmetic progressions then $\lvert A\rvert \leq \exp(-c(\log N)^{1/9})N$ for some $c>0$
claims.skeptic_note: Fetched arxiv.org/abs/2309.02353. Abstract confirms verbatim: 'if A subset {1,...,N} has no non-trivial three-term arithmetic progressions then |A| <= exp(-c(log N)^{1/9})N for some c>0.' Matches claim and formula exactly.

claims.claim: Green and Tao (2017, arXiv 1705.01703) proved a polylogarithmic bound r_4(N) << N(log N)^{-c}, improving on Gowers's 1998 double-log bound and their own 2005 bound; they state this appears to be the limit of their method, and the constant c is asserted to exist ('some absolute constant c>0') but is not given an explicit numeric value in the abstract/intro.
claims.formula: r_4(N) \ll N(\log N)^{-c} for some absolute constant c>0
claims.citation: Ben Green, Terence Tao, "New bounds for Szemerédi's theorem, III: A polylogarithmic bound for r_4(N)," arXiv:1705.01703, published in Mathematika
claims.quote: Define r₄(N) to be the largest cardinality of a set A ⊂ {1,…,N} which does not contain four elements in arithmetic progression. In 1998 Gowers proved that r₄(N) ≪ N(log log N)^(-c) for some absolute constant c>0. In 2005, the authors improved this to r₄(N) ≪ N e^(-c√log log N). In this paper we further improve this to r₄(N) ≪ N(log N)^(-c), which appears to be the limit of our methods.
claims.skeptic_note: Fetched arxiv.org/abs/1705.01703. Abstract states verbatim: 'In 1998 Gowers proved that r4(N) << N(log log N)^{-c}... In 2005 ... N e^{-c sqrt(log log N)}. In this paper we further improve this to r4(N) << N(log N)^{-c}, which appears to be the limit of our methods.' All formulas, prior bounds, and the 'limit of our methods' statement match exactly. The claim's characterization that no explicit numeric value of c is given (only 'some absolute constant c>0', asserted for the 1998 bound and implicitly carried through) is also accurate -- no numeric constant appears anywhere in the abstract.

claims.topic: Green-Tao paper intro - equivalence to Erdos's conjecture (r_k(2^n)/2^n series)
claims.claim: The Green-Tao paper's introduction explicitly states the reduction: Erdos's conjecture on divergent-reciprocal-sum sets is equivalent to the convergence of the series sum_n r_k(2^n)/2^n for all k>=3.
claims.citation: Ben Green, Terence Tao, "New bounds for Szemerédi's theorem, III: A polylogarithmic bound for r_4(N)," arXiv:1705.01703, introduction (fetched via ar5iv HTML rendering)
claims.quote: It is worth noting that the famous conjecture of Erdős asserting that every set of natural numbers whose sum of reciprocals is divergent is equivalent to the claim that ∑n=1∞rk(2n)2n<∞ for all k⩾3.
claims.skeptic_note: Fetched ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1705.01703. Introduction contains verbatim: 'It is worth noting that the famous conjecture of Erdos asserting that every set of natural numbers whose sum of reciprocals is divergent is equivalent to the claim that sum_{n=1}^infty r_k(2^n)/2^n < infinity for all k >= 3.' Exact match.

claims.topic: Green-Tao paper - no explicit Tao-Vu citation found in fetched excerpt
claims.claim: In the ar5iv-rendered introduction text that was actually fetched, no mention of 'Tao-Vu' (a citation to a book/paper by Tao and Vu) was found. This does not rule out such a citation existing elsewhere in the paper (e.g. bibliography, a section not captured in the fetch); it is reported as not confirmed on the page actually retrieved.
claims.citation: Ben Green, Terence Tao, arXiv:1705.01703, introduction (ar5iv rendering) — negative/unconfirmed finding
claims.quote: No mention of "Tao-Vu" appears in the provided excerpt.
claims.skeptic_note: This is a self-reported negative finding by the other researcher (their own verified_by_fetch flag is already false). I independently searched the same ar5iv-rendered page for 'Tao-Vu' / 'Tao and Vu' and found no such mention anywhere in the fetched content, consistent with the claim as stated. The claim is appropriately hedged ('does not rule out ... existing elsewhere').

claims.topic: No known improvement to r_4(N) bound after Green-Tao (2017), through searches performed
claims.claim: No paper improving on the Green-Tao r_4(N) ≪ N(log N)^{-c} bound was found in the sources checked (erdosproblems.com problem page and forum thread, targeted WebSearches). erdosproblems.com's own summary of best-known bounds (fetched 2026-09-27) still lists Green-Tao as the current bound for k=4, with Leng-Sah-Sawhney only covering k≥5.
claims.formula: r_4(N) \ll N(\log N)^{-c} (unimproved, per sources checked)
claims.citation: erdosproblems.com Problem #3 page (fetched 2026-09-27); WebSearch queries for r_4(N) improvements 2024-2025
claims.quote: Green-Tao (k=4): "$r_4(N)\ll N/(\log N)^{c}$ for some small constant $c>0$"
claims.skeptic_note: Fetched erdosproblems.com/3 directly for the Green-Tao line: verbatim 'Green and Tao [GrTa17] proved r_4(N) << N/(log N)^c for some small constant c>0' -- matches quote exactly. The page discusses k=3 (Bloom-Sisask, Kelley-Meka) and k=4 (Green-Tao) as separate, better-than-general-k results, then presents the Leng-Sah-Sawhney bound as the 'current best bounds for general k' -- consistent with Leng-Sah-Sawhney's own paper (arXiv:2402.17995), whose abstract explicitly restricts its result to k>=5 ('We show that for k>=5, there exists c_k>0 such that...'). An independent WebSearch for 2024-2025 improvements to r_4(N) turned up no result superseding Green-Tao 2017, corroborating the negative finding. No resolution or improvement to the Green-Tao r_4(N) bound was found in any source checked.

claims.topic: Leng-Sah-Sawhney 2024 - best known bound for r_k(N), k>=5
claims.claim: Leng, Sah, and Sawhney (2024) proved r_k(N) << N exp(-(log log N)^{c_k}) for k>=5 and some c_k>0, the current best general bound, improving on Gowers's earlier N/(log log N)^{c_k} type bound; they rely on quasipolynomial Gowers-norm inverse theorem bounds and the Heath-Brown/Szemeredi density increment strategy as reformulated by Green-Tao. The abstract does not give an explicit value/formula for c_k, only asserts its existence.
claims.formula: r_k(N) \ll N\exp(-(\log\log N)^{c_k}) for some constant c_k>0, for k \ge 5
claims.citation: James Leng, Ashwin Sah, Mehtaab Sawhney, "Improved Bounds for Szemerédi's Theorem," arXiv:2402.17995 (2024)
claims.quote: The authors note their proof relies on "recent quasipolynomial bounds on the inverse theorem for the Gowers $U^k$-norm as well as the density increment strategy of Heath-Brown and Szemerédi as reformulated by Green and Tao."
claims.skeptic_note: Fetched arxiv.org/abs/2402.17995 verbatim: 'We show that for k>=5, there exists c_k>0 such that r_k(N) << N exp(-(log log N)^{c_k}). Our proof is a consequence of recent quasipolynomial bounds on the inverse theorem for the Gowers U^k-norm as well as the density increment strategy of Heath-Brown and Szemeredi as reformulated by Green and Tao.' The bolded/quoted portion of the claim's quote matches this verbatim; formula, k>=5 restriction, and the non-explicit c_k are all accurate.

claims.topic: erdosproblems.com's own statement of the Leng-Sah-Sawhney bound
claims.claim: erdosproblems.com's Problem 3 page states the current best general-k bound as r_k(N) << N/exp((log log N)^{c_k}), attributed to Leng, Sah, Sawhney.
claims.quote: Leng-Sah-Sawhney (current best, general k): "$r_k(N) \ll \frac{N}{\exp((\log\log N)^{c_k})}$ for constant $c_k>0$"
claims.skeptic_note: Fetched erdosproblems.com/3. The page presents this in prose, not as a labeled table row: 'The current best bounds for general k are due to Leng, Sah, and Sawhney [LSS24], who show that r_k(N) << N/exp((log log N)^{c_k}) for some constant c_k>0 depending on k.' The formula and attribution in the claim match exactly, but the claim's quote format ('Leng-Sah-Sawhney (current best, general k): "..."') is a paraphrased/reformatted rendering rather than a verbatim excerpt -- the page uses running prose, not a table with that label.
claims.corrected_claim: erdosproblems.com's Problem 3 page states, in prose (not a table): 'The current best bounds for general k are due to Leng, Sah, and Sawhney [LSS24], who show that r_k(N) \ll N/\exp((\log\log N)^{c_k}) for some constant c_k>0 depending on k.' The formula and attribution are accurate; only the tabular quote formatting is an editorial paraphrase, not a verbatim page excerpt.

claims.topic: No 2024-2026 result proving convergence of sum r_k(N)/N^2 for any k>=4, no claimed resolution of Erdos 3
claims.claim: No source found in this research (erdosproblems.com Problem 3 page, its forum thread #3, ProofAtlas's Erdos-Turan collaboration page, and multiple targeted WebSearches covering 2024-2026) reports a proof that r_k(N) ≪ N/(log N)^{1+c} for any k>=4 (equivalently that Sum r_k(N)/N^2 < infinity for some k>=4), nor any claimed resolution of Erdos Problem 3 for k>=4 or in general. The forum thread's only two comments (Sep 4, 2025) concern an unrelated technical counterexample question about 'consecutive terms,' not a resolution claim. ProofAtlas explicitly states the general conjecture (all finite lengths) remains open as of its last content.
claims.citation: erdosproblems.com/3; erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/3; proofatlas.ai Erdos-Turan Arithmetic Progressions Conjecture page
claims.quote: This is false even for k=3. For example take all integers congruent to 0 or 1 [modulo 3]
claims.skeptic_note: Fetched erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/3. It contains exactly two comments: Dogmachine (04 Sep 2025, 21:28) asking about a stronger 'consecutive terms' variant, and Thomas Bloom (04 Sep 2025, 21:41) replying verbatim 'This is false even for k=3. For example take all integers congruent to 0 or 1 modulo 3.' No resolution claim appears in the thread, matching the claim exactly. (ProofAtlas page separately confirmed under c13.)

claims.topic: ProofAtlas summary confirming k=3 only, general conjecture open
claims.claim: ProofAtlas's collaboration page on the Erdos-Turan conjecture states the reciprocal-sum conjecture is solved only for three-term progressions via quantitative Roth-type bounds, while the assertion for progressions of every finite length remains open, with no claimed proof of the full conjecture.
claims.citation: ProofAtlas, "Erdős–Turán Conjecture on Arithmetic Progressions" collaboration page
claims.quote: The reciprocal-sum conjecture is solved for three-term progressions through quantitative Roth-type bounds, but the assertion that every divergent-reciprocal-sum set contains progressions of every finite length remains open.
claims.skeptic_note: Fetched proofatlas.ai collaboration page. It states verbatim: 'The reciprocal-sum conjecture is solved for three-term progressions through quantitative Roth-type bounds, but the assertion that every divergent-reciprocal-sum set contains progressions of every finite length remains open.' Exact match to the claim and quote.
